title: When things go wrong
topic: complaining and solving a problem politely; at the doctor's
why: This last lesson on travel gives you the words for when things go wrong: something that doesn't work, a lost or stolen object, a visit to the doctor or the pharmacy. You'll complain politely with Pourriez-vous… ? and say what hurts with avoir mal à.

{"lessons": ["

Something's wrong: complaining politely

A broken shower, a noisy room, a lost key: when things go wrong on a trip, the French expect you to stay polite, even when you complain. Start with Excusez-moi or Bonjour (never skip it!), then describe the problem.

FrenchEnglish
Il y a un problème avec la chambre.There's a problem with the room.
La douche ne marche pas.The shower doesn't work.
Le chauffage ne fonctionne pas.The heating isn't working.
Il n'y a pas d'eau chaude.There's no hot water.
La chambre est sale / très bruyante.The room is dirty / very noisy.
Je voudrais me plaindre.I'd like to make a complaint.

For a machine or an object, \"to work\" is marcher (everyday) or fonctionner (a bit more formal). Never travailler, which is only for people: Mon téléphone ne marche pas, but Mon frère ne travaille pas le lundi.

Pourriez-vous… ? The polite request

To ask for a solution, use Pourriez-vous… ? + infinitive (Could you…?). Take it as a fixed polite formula for now: it's the conditional of pouvoir, which you'll study in unit 11.

Pourriez-vous m'aider, s'il vous plaît ?Could you help me, please?
Pourriez-vous appeler un technicien ?Could you call a technician?
Pourriez-vous me donner une autre chambre ?Could you give me another room?

Pourriez-vous is softer than Pouvez-vous, which is softer than an imperative. In a hotel or a shop, a polite tone gets things fixed much faster.

", "

Lost and stolen

To tell what happened, you need the passé composé. With avoir: J'ai perdu mon passeport (I've lost my passport). With être: Je suis tombé / Je suis tombée (I fell).

J'ai perdu mes clés. J'ai cherché partout, mais je ne les trouve pas.I've lost my keys. I've looked everywhere, but I can't find them.

On m'a volé… : someone stole…

When you don't know who did it, French uses on (someone): On m'a volé mon portefeuille = Someone stole my wallet / My wallet was stolen. Learn it as a fixed phrase: m' means \"from me\" here.

FrenchEnglish
On m'a volé mon sac.My bag was stolen.
On m'a volé ma carte bancaire.My bank card was stolen.
J'ai perdu mon téléphone dans le métro.I lost my phone on the metro.
Où est le commissariat ?Where is the police station?

Watch out: voler has two meanings, \"to steal\" and \"to fly\". Les oiseaux volent = Birds fly. Context always makes it clear.

At the police station, you'll describe the object with what you know: C'est un sac noir, assez grand. Il y avait mon passeport dedans. (There was my passport in it.) The imparfait describes, the passé composé tells what happened: J'étais dans le bus quand on m'a volé mon portefeuille.

For a lost card, call your bank right away: in French this is faire opposition (to cancel / block a card). You'll hear it at the bank and at the police station.

", "

At the doctor's and the pharmacy

To say what hurts, French uses avoir mal à + the definite article: J'ai mal à la tête (literally \"I have pain at the head\"). English says \"my head hurts\" or \"I have a headache\", with a possessive; French uses le, la, les, never ma tête. Don't forget the contractions: à + le = au, à + les = aux.

FrenchEnglish
J'ai mal à la tête.I have a headache.
J'ai mal à la gorge.I have a sore throat.
J'ai mal au dos / au ventre.My back hurts / I have a stomachache.
J'ai mal aux dents / aux pieds.I have a toothache / My feet hurt.
J'ai de la fièvre.I have a fever.
Je tousse.I'm coughing.
Je suis enrhumé / enrhumée.I have a cold.

Seeing a doctor

In France you first see le médecin généraliste (the family doctor, GP). You make un rendez-vous (an appointment) and leave with une ordonnance (a prescription), which you take to la pharmacie. At night and on Sundays, look for la pharmacie de garde (the on-duty pharmacy).

The doctor's advice comes in the imperative: Prenez un comprimé trois fois par jour, Reposez-vous, Buvez beaucoup d'eau.

J'ai mal à la gorge et je tousse depuis trois jours.I have a sore throat and I've been coughing for three days.

False friend: une prescription exists in French, but the paper the doctor gives you is une ordonnance. And French pharmacists give real advice: for a small problem, ask them first.
